file: papers/pdf/Ma - 2002 - Competitive Advantage What's Luck Got to Do with It.pdf
about: A conceptual paper on luck as a source of firm competitive advantage. It offers a typology of luck (pure luck, prepared luck, useful weeds, skunk work), the external sources of luck, and the internal mechanisms by which firms can induce, recognise and exploit lucky breaks.

This final part of Hao Ma's paper on luck and competitive advantage contains only the tail of the reference list and three end-of-article application questions, such as the link between the luck typology and competitive advantage, and profiting from 'useful weeds' and skunk-work initiatives.

candidates.label: Luck as serendipitous happening
candidates.definition: The author treats luck as serendipitous happenings that are unpredictable beforehand and often unfathomable even to those who benefit. Luck arises from both chance events and human endeavour.
candidates.applies_when: An account describes an unpredictable, unplanned happening that benefited the venture, and the person treats it as luck or chance.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The benefit was planned and foreseen from the start, with no chance element.

candidates.label: Serendipity as opportunity seized
candidates.definition: Luck is usually opportunities knocking on those who are looking for them, notice them and act on them. Serendipity counts only when the opportunity is seized and its potential realised.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes noticing a chance opportunity and acting on it, and the benefit came from that action.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: A windfall arrived without any noticing or action by the person; code that as pure luck.

candidates.label: Pure luck
candidates.definition: Factors outside the firm produce an advantage spontaneously, beyond the firm's purposeful control or manipulation. Examples are fertile land, oil underneath it, or a windfall gain from someone else's loss.
candidates.applies_when: An account describes an external windfall that benefited the venture without any foresight or action on its part.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The firm had positioned itself or acted to capture the event; code that as prepared luck.

candidates.label: Prepared luck
candidates.definition: External changes act as mere opportunities or threats. Whether a firm turns out lucky depends on its position, endowments, capabilities and action at the time. Here random forces validate foresight and purposeful action.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes an external change that benefited the venture because of prior preparation, foresight or quick action.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The gain required no action or capability of the firm (pure luck).

candidates.label: Useful weeds
candidates.definition: Self-initiated activities by individuals inside the firm, such as experiments or improvisations pursued for whatever motives. They sometimes yield accidental innovations, for example a spilled liquid that was tasted or a 'failed' weak adhesive.
candidates.applies_when: An account describes an accidental discovery made by an individual during side activity, personal experimentation or a failed project.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The work was an organised, secret group effort pursuing a deliberate goal; code that as skunk work.

candidates.label: Skunk work
candidates.definition: Individuals or informal groups work voluntarily and secretively on their own initiative, independent of or against the formal agenda. This is a semi-grass-roots effort that may bring lucky breaks or disaster.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes a secret or informal side project pursued outside official plans that led to an unexpected venture or breakthrough.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The initiative was organisation-wide and explicitly endorsed by top management (managerial initiative).

candidates.label: Unique historical or crisis events
candidates.definition: International, political, economic or military events can bring luck. Examples include the oil crisis, the Gulf War, 9/11 and a city fire.
candidates.applies_when: A venture's opportunity is attributed to an unexpected major event or crisis.

candidates.label: Shifts in culture, taste or technology
candidates.definition: Changes in social-cultural trends, customer tastes or technology can spell luck for some firms and disaster for others. For example, technological change gives lucky breaks to small but ambitious firms.
candidates.applies_when: An account attributes the venture's opportunity to an unforeseen change in trends, customer preferences or technology.

candidates.label: Regulation or deregulation
candidates.definition: New government rules or deregulation can unexpectedly create markets or openings for certain firms. Examples are mandatory fire equipment after a fire and bank expansion after deregulation.
candidates.applies_when: A venture's opportunity arose from an unexpected regulatory change.

candidates.label: Asymmetric information or rival ignorance
candidates.definition: Private information, or a rival's ignorance and negligence, can open a window of opportunity. An example is a seller not knowing about the IBM deal.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes benefiting by chance from knowing something others did not, or from a rival's oversight.

candidates.label: Faltering competitor or dream expediter
candidates.definition: Luck can arrive when a competitor falters, for example through bankruptcy or the death of a founder. It can also arrive through the unexpected appearance of a badly needed partner, supplier, complementor or talented person.
candidates.applies_when: An account credits the venture's progress to a competitor's unexpected failure, or to a chance encounter with a key partner or person.

candidates.label: Alertness and scanning
candidates.definition: Being constantly alert, scanning the environment and spotting trends helps a firm recognise chance opportunities and capture windfall gains.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes habitually watching for opportunities and spotting one when it appeared.

candidates.label: Quick decisive action on chance
candidates.definition: Luck favours those in action. Seizing an opportunity quickly and aggressively, with a sense of urgency, turns a chance event into advantage.
candidates.applies_when: An account describes rapid action on an unexpected opportunity, such as borrowing funds immediately or acting aggressively.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The person noticed the opportunity but did not act on it.

candidates.label: Commercialising unintended innovations
candidates.definition: Accidental discoveries remain 'weeds' until they are channelled toward the right customer markets or activities. Managers must notice them and proactively exploit their commercial potential.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes taking an accidental invention or discovery and finding a market or use for it.

candidates.label: Championing and seducing elites
candidates.definition: Grass-roots initiatives need champions and middle managers who spot them, frame them as future advantage, and win resources and protection from decision-makers.
candidates.applies_when: An account describes someone sponsoring, protecting or selling a chance-born initiative to gain support and resources.

candidates.label: Prepared mind and position
candidates.definition: Whether chance yields advantage depends on the firm's existing position, endowments, capabilities and foresight. Luck favours the prepared mind.
candidates.applies_when: The person links the ability to benefit from a chance event to prior knowledge, skills or resources already held.

candidates.label: Expert contacts
candidates.definition: Maintaining active contacts with experts helps firms make sense of events, predict threats and gain from lucky opportunities.
candidates.applies_when: An account mentions relying on expert networks or contacts to interpret an unexpected event and exploit it.

candidates.label: Organisational slack
candidates.definition: A certain level of slack is needed to allow self-initiated actions, experiments and improvisation, from which unexpected gains sometimes come.
candidates.applies_when: The person mentions having free time, resources or leeway to experiment, which led to an accidental discovery.

candidates.label: Open-mindedness and tolerance for error
candidates.definition: Open-mindedness, tolerance for errors and a culture that dares people to experiment and fail make serendipitous gains more likely to be realised.
candidates.applies_when: An account credits openness to failure or experimentation with enabling an unexpected success.

candidates.label: Structure as hotbed of innovation
candidates.definition: Structures and cultures that encourage autonomous innovation make useful weeds and skunk work more likely. One example is letting a new product become its own division.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes an organisational setting whose autonomy or structure fostered side initiatives that led to new ventures.

candidates.label: Proactive versus passive posture
candidates.definition: Some firms wait passively for lucky breaks, while others seek them proactively. A proactive firm is more aware of when it could get lucky and better at exploiting luck. Waiting for luck passively is a disservice.
candidates.applies_when: An account contrasts actively seeking chance opportunities with simply waiting for them.

candidates.label: Overconfidence and complacency
candidates.definition: Arrogance, ignorance, negligence, overconfidence or complacency in the face of luck reduce the ability to benefit from it. Failing firms are often clueless in times of change rather than unlucky.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes missing or squandering a chance opportunity through complacency, arrogance or inattention.

candidates.label: Competitive advantage and new products
candidates.definition: Serendipity can yield competitive advantage in the form of new products, processes, knowledge or capabilities, and sometimes whole new businesses. It can equally result in waste, redundancy and failure.
candidates.applies_when: An account links a chance event or discovery to a new product, business line or advantage, or to wasted effort.

candidates.label: Redirecting the venture
candidates.definition: Accidental or skunk-work innovations may not fit the current business scope. They can call for new strategic directions and change the course of the firm.
candidates.applies_when: A chance discovery or opportunity is described as changing the venture's direction or strategy.

candidates.label: Luck as deserved or earned
candidates.definition: Beneficiaries often believe they deserved their luck. What outsiders see as luck may be the outcome of systematic, visionary effort duly rewarded, so that 'luck is created'.
candidates.applies_when: The person narrates a lucky outcome as earned or deserved, or as the product of their own effort and vision.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The person attributes the outcome purely to chance.

candidates.label: Retrospective reframing as lucky
candidates.definition: Events can be reinterpreted afterwards as lucky incidents. New Coke, for example, came to be seen as providing lessons and publicity.
candidates.applies_when: The person reframes a setback or mistake, in hindsight, as a lucky turn.

candidates.label: Vision and insider knowledge, not chance
candidates.definition: Luck can be read as vision meeting opportunity. To those who know the behind-the-scenes story, success is never an entirely random process.
candidates.applies_when: An account suggests that an apparently lucky outcome is better explained by foresight, planning or insider knowledge.
